title: Trigonometry Applications: Heights, Distances & Triangle Rules (Practice Problems + Free Quiz)
meta_title: Trigonometry Applications: Practice Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master trigonometry applications: heights and distances, angle of elevation and depression, plus the sine and cosine rules, with a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Most students can recite sin, cos and tan but freeze when a question asks for the height of a tower. The gap is not the formula — it is setting up the diagram. Here is how to do that cleanly, with worked examples and a quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Suppose the flag pole in your school ground needs a new rope and nobody fancies climbing it to measure the height. You can still find it to the nearest centimetre without leaving the ground: walk out 15 m, sight the top through a straw fixed to a protractor, read the angle, and one line of maths hands you the answer. That is the entire idea behind trigonometry applications — turning an angle you can measure into a length you cannot reach. Most students can recite the ratios; where marks are lost is in the set-up.

This is a Class 11 and 12 staple, and it splits neatly into two families of problems: heights and distances (which live inside right-angled triangles) and the properties of triangles (the sine and cosine rules, for triangles that are not right-angled). Get comfortable with both and a whole chapter of the exam becomes routine.

Start with the diagram, every single time

I have marked enough scripts to say this plainly: the students who draw a clear figure first almost never get the wrong ratio, and the ones who jump straight to numbers almost always do. Before you touch a calculator, sketch the situation and label three things.

  • The horizontal line (usually the ground) and the vertical object standing on it.
  • The angle and exactly where it sits — at the eye of the observer, not at the top of the tower.
  • Which side you know and which side you want, relative to that angle: opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse.

Those three labels decide everything that follows. Skip them and you are guessing.

Angle of elevation and angle of depression

The angle of elevation is how far you tilt your line of sight up from the horizontal to look at something higher — the top of a tower, a kite, an aircraft. The angle of depression is how far you tilt down from the horizontal to look at something lower, like a boat seen from a cliff.

Here is the fact that saves time: the angle of depression from the top of an object equals the angle of elevation from the point below it. They are alternate angles between two parallel horizontals, so they are always equal. The common mistake is drawing the depression angle inside the triangle at the wrong corner — it belongs at the observer’s eye, measured from the horizontal through that eye.

Choosing the right ratio

Once the diagram is labelled, picking the ratio is mechanical. The old memory aid still works: SOH-CAH-TOA — Sine is Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse, Tangent is Opposite over Adjacent. In most heights-and-distances questions you know a horizontal distance (adjacent) and want a vertical height (opposite), so tangent does the heavy lifting.

Take the classic case. From a point 30 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of the top is 60°. Height and horizontal distance are opposite and adjacent to the 60° angle, so use tangent: tan 60° = height ÷ 30. Since tan 60° = √3, the height is 30√3 ≈ 51.96 m. No climbing required.

Two-observer problems

The step up in difficulty is when a single angle is not enough and you observe the same object from two points. These look intimidating but reduce to two right triangles sharing the same height.

A tower is seen from two points on level ground, in line with its base. From the nearer point the angle of elevation is 60°; from the farther point, 30°. The two points are 20 m apart. Call the height h and the nearer distance x. Then h = x tan 60° and h = (x + 20) tan 30°. Setting them equal gives x√3 = (x + 20)÷√3, so 3x = x + 20, which means x = 10. The height is 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m. The trick is always the shared side — write the height two ways and equate.

When the triangle is not right-angled: sine and cosine rules

Real triangles are rarely obliging enough to contain a right angle. For those, the properties-of-triangles toolkit takes over. For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C:

  • Sine rule: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. Use it when you have an angle paired with its opposite side, plus one more piece.
  • Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides.

Worked cosine example: a triangle has sides b = 8 and c = 5 with the included angle A = 60°. Then a² = 64 + 25 − 2 × 8 × 5 × cos 60° = 89 − 40 = 49, so a = 7. Clean numbers like these are a hint from the examiner that you have chosen the right rule.

A quick decision table

What you haveTool to reach forTypical question
Right triangle, height and distancetan (or sin / cos)Height of a tower from one point
Same object, two viewpointsTwo right triangles, equate the heightElevation 60° and 30°, points 20 m apart
Angle opposite a known sideSine ruleFind a missing angle or side
Two sides and the included angleCosine ruleFind the third side
All three sidesCosine rule (rearranged)Find any angle

One honest caveat for exams: the sine rule can be ambiguous when you are given two sides and a non-included angle — there are sometimes two valid triangles. If the numbers allow it, always check whether the obtuse case also fits. Examiners love that trap.

Test yourself, then get more practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz built around exactly these ideas — elevation and depression, choosing the ratio, two-observer set-ups, and the sine and cosine rules. Try each one, then read the explanation for anything you miss. When you want the harder, exam-style problems that separate a 90 from a 99, the NCERT Exemplar solutions in the box below work through them step by step.

quiz.title: Trigonometry Applications Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on heights and distances, angle of elevation and depression, and the sine and cosine rules. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Applications of trigonometry: heights, distances and triangle rules

questions.q: From a point 25 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of the top is 45°. How tall is the tower?
questions.explanation: Height and distance are opposite and adjacent to 45°, so use tangent. tan 45° = 1, so height = 25 × 1 = 25 m.

questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a 60 m tower from a point on the ground is 30°. How far is that point from the foot of the tower?
questions.explanation: tan 30° = height ÷ distance = 60 ÷ d. Since tan 30° = 1÷√3, d = 60√3 ≈ 103.9 m.

questions.q: The angle of depression of a boat seen from the top of a lighthouse is 40°. What is the angle of elevation of the lighthouse top as seen from the boat?
questions.explanation: The angle of depression and the angle of elevation are alternate angles between parallel horizontals, so they are equal: 40°.

questions.q: A tower is seen from two points in line with its base. From the nearer point the elevation is 60°, from the farther point 30°, and the points are 20 m apart. How tall is the tower?
questions.explanation: Write the height two ways: h = x tan 60° and h = (x + 20) tan 30°. Solving gives x = 10, so h = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 m.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, side a = 6, angle A = 30° and angle B = 90°. Using the sine rule, find side b.
questions.explanation: By the sine rule, b = a × sin B ÷ sin A = 6 × 1 ÷ 0.5 = 12.

questions.q: In triangle ABC, b = 8, c = 5 and the included angle A = 60°. Find side a.
questions.explanation: Cosine rule: a² = 8² + 5² − 2 × 8 × 5 × cos 60° = 89 − 40 = 49, so a = 7.

questions.q: You know the side opposite an angle and the hypotenuse of a right triangle and want the angle. Which ratio do you use?
questions.explanation: Opposite over hypotenuse is the sine ratio, so sin of the angle = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.

questions.q: A 12 m ladder leans against a wall, making a 60° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
questions.explanation: The height is opposite the 60° angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so height = 12 sin 60° = 12 × (√3 ÷ 2) = 6√3 ≈ 10.39 m.

faq.q: When do I use the sine rule and when the cosine rule?
faq.a: Use the sine rule when you have an angle together with the side opposite it, plus one more side or angle. Use the cosine rule when you know two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides and want an angle.

faq.q: Are the angle of elevation and angle of depression ever equal?
faq.a: Yes, and this is worth remembering. The angle of depression from the top of an object to a point below equals the angle of elevation from that point back up to the top — they are alternate angles between parallel horizontal lines.

faq.q: Why do so many students lose marks in heights and distances?
faq.a: Almost always because they skip the diagram or place the angle at the wrong corner. Draw the figure, mark the angle at the observer’s eye, and label each side as opposite, adjacent or hypotenuse before choosing a ratio.

faq.q: Do I need a calculator for these problems in exams?
faq.a: Usually the angles are the standard ones — 30°, 45° and 60° — whose sine, cosine and tangent values you should know by heart. Answers are often left in surd form like 10√3, so a calculator is rarely essential.

faq.q: Where can I get more exam-style practice problems with full solutions?
faq.a: The NCERT Exemplar Problems and Solutions for Class 12 Mathematics cover applications of trigonometry with step-by-step worked answers, from single-observer heights to multi-triangle set-ups. It is an instant PDF you can print and revise from — the link is in the box below.
